``` # Objectives and overview This course builds on the chapter on hypotheses and tests and continues our exploration of inferential statistics through ANOVA, interactions, experimental design, linear mixed models and bootstrap. Each section combines an explanation, executable R code, and graphs. By the end of the session, you should be able to: - compare several means and interpret the F statistic; - check a model’s assumptions and choose a suitable alternative; - distinguish main effects from an interaction between two factors; - construct a completely randomised design, a Latin square and a block design; - distinguish fixed and random effects in a linear mixed model; - estimate uncertainty using bootstrap while respecting the sampling unit. # Preparing for the session ## Installing packages Packages only need to be installed once in the R console: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 1: Install any missing packages packages = c("ggplot2", "readxl", "emmeans", "lme4", "lmerTest", "boot") for (pkg in packages) { if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages(pkg) } library(pkg, character.only = TRUE) } # Set a theme for ggplot graphs theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13)) # Create a function to calculate a t-based confidence interval for the mean, without depending on the Hmisc package. ic_moyenne <- function(x) { x <- x[is.finite(x)] marge <- qt(.975, df = length(x) - 1) * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)) data.frame(y = mean(x), ymin = mean(x) - marge, ymax = mean(x) + marge) } # Set global options for the session options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"), digits = 4) # Set a seed for random draws. set.seed(2026) ``` ::: ## Importing and checking the data The file **data 2025.xlsx** contains the sheets `data`, `clean` and `legend`. ``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/proxy/320471/VK2KexpLPIQork1l.mp4?width=1920&height=1080&start=0). ::: ## Question, hypotheses and model **Question:** is mean life expectancy the same in every region? For $k$ regions, the null hypothesis is $H_0 : \mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k$. The alternative is that at least one mean differs. The model is: $$Y_{ij}=\mu+\alpha_i+\varepsilon_{ij}.$$ $Y_{ij}$ is the life expectancy of country $j$ in region $i$, $\mu$ is a reference level and $\alpha_i$ is the effect of the region. ANOVA compares **between-group** variability with **residual variability within groups**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 4 # Boxplot for each group ggplot(data_2025 , aes(region, lex, fill = region)) + geom_boxplot(width = .55, alpha = .45, outlier.shape = NA) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .12, seed = 1), alpha = .55) + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "white") + labs(x = "Region", y = "Life expectancy (years)") + guides(fill = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/description-regions-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The boxes describe the distributions, and the white diamonds show the means. A visual difference alone does not quantify uncertainty or reveal its cause. ## Decomposing variance and calculating F $$SS_{total}=SS_{between}+SS_{residual}, \qquad F=\frac{SS_{between}/(k-1)}{SS_{residual}/(n-k)}.$$ Under the model’s assumptions and $H_0$, this statistic follows an F distribution with $k-1$ and $n-k$ degrees of freedom. A high value indicates that differences between means are large relative to the residual variation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 5: One-way ANOVA # Calculate the ANOVA with the aov function d <- data_2025 m1 <- aov(lex ~ region, data = d) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) region 3 4852 1617 70.3 <2e-16 *** Residuals 188 4327 23 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate the ANOVA step by step n <- nrow(d) k <- nlevels(as.factor(d$region)) moyennes <- ave(d$lex, d$region, FUN = mean) ss_entre <- sum((moyennes - mean(d$lex))^2) ss_res <- sum((d$lex - moyennes)^2) F_calcule <- (ss_entre / (k - 1)) / (ss_res / (n - k)) p_calcule <- pf(F_calcule, k - 1, n - k, lower.tail = FALSE) knitr::kable(data.frame(F = F_calcule, df1 = k - 1, df2 = n - k, p.value = p_calcule)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | F| df1| df2| p.value| |-----:|---:|---:|-------:| | 70.28| 3| 188| 0| ::: ::: A small p-value indicates incompatibility with all means being equal, under the model. It does not identify which regions differ or measure the size of the difference. ## Checking the assumptions Classical ANOVA assumes independent errors with a common variance and an approximately normal distribution for exact inference. Normality concerns the **conditional errors**, examined through the residuals, rather than the distribution of all observations pooled together. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 7: Diagnostics ancien <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(m1, which = 1) plot(m1, which = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/diagnostics-anova-1.png){width=864} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(ancien) shapiro.test(residuals(m1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shapiro-Wilk normality test data: residuals(m1) W = 0.99, p-value = 0.1 ``` ::: ::: The residuals-versus-fitted-values plot helps identify differences in spread and unusual values. The QQ plot examines the shape of the residual distribution. ## Which regions differ? Running multiple t-tests without adjustment increases the risk of at least one false positive. Tukey comparisons control this risk across the family of pairwise comparisons under the classical assumptions. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 8: Tukey test comparaisons <- TukeyHSD(m1) comparaisons ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Tukey multiple comparisons of means 95% family-wise confidence level Fit: aov(formula = lex ~ region, data = d) $region diff lwr upr p adj americas-africa 9.556 6.857 12.254 0.0000 asia-africa 7.965 5.604 10.327 0.0000 europe-africa 13.506 11.011 16.001 0.0000 asia-americas -1.590 -4.261 1.080 0.4136 europe-americas 3.950 1.161 6.739 0.0018 europe-asia 5.541 3.076 8.005 0.0000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} plot(comparaisons, las = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/tukey-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: An interval for a difference that excludes zero indicates a difference detected with the Tukey adjustment. ## A rank-based alternative Kruskal–Wallis compares distributions using ranks. In general, it does not test equality of means or only equality of medians. Interpreting it as a shift in location requires, among other things, distributions with comparable shapes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 9: Kruskal–Wallis test kruskal.test(lex ~ region, data = d) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test data: lex by region Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 99, df = 3, p-value <2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pairwise.wilcox.test(d$lex, d$region, p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pairwise comparisons using Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction data: d$lex and d$region africa americas asia americas 2e-10 - - asia 2e-09 0.08 - europe 1e-15 2e-05 2e-06 P value adjustment method: holm ``` ::: ::: # Two-way ANOVA and interactions ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/proxy/320472/UPvMPZKH7KS74ICF.mp4?width=1920&height=1080&start=0). ::: ## When the effect of one factor depends on another This example uses adult height by sex and two fictional nationalities, A and B. These categories are used only to explain the calculation. We simulate individuals because the country-level workbook does not contain this experimental structure. $$Y_{ijk}=\mu+\alpha_i+\beta_j+(\alpha\beta)_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ijk}.$$ In R, `sexe * nationalite` expands to `sexe + nationalite + sexe:nationalite`. Without an interaction, the difference between sexes stays constant across nationalities. With an interaction, this difference changes. Lines can be non-parallel without crossing. ## Simulating the two situations, with and without interaction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 10: Interactions simuler_tailles <- function(moyennes, graine) { set.seed(graine) z <- expand.grid(individu = seq_len(40), sexe = c("F", "H"), nationalite = c("A", "B")) z$sexe <- factor(z$sexe, levels = c("F", "H")) z$nationalite <- factor(z$nationalite, levels = c("A", "B")) cle <- paste(z$sexe, z$nationalite, sep = "_") z$taille <- unname(moyennes[cle]) + rnorm(nrow(z), sd = 4) z } sans <- simuler_tailles(c(F_A = 162, H_A = 174, F_B = 170, H_B = 182), 31) avec <- simuler_tailles(c(F_A = 160, H_A = 176, F_B = 172, H_B = 180), 32) sans$situation <- "No interaction in the generating model" avec$situation <- "Interaction in the generating model" tailles <- rbind(sans, avec) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 11: Interaction plot ggplot(tailles, aes(nationalite, taille, color = sexe, group = sexe)) + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 1) + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) + stat_summary(fun.data = ic_moyenne, geom = "errorbar", width = .08) + facet_wrap(~ situation) + labs(x = "Fictional nationality", y = "Height (cm)", color = "Sex") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Observed means and 95% confidence intervals for each cell mean. Sampling variation can make the lines slightly non-parallel even without a theoretical interaction.](index-en-r_files/figure-html/fig-interactions-1.png){#fig-interactions width=960} ::: ::: ## Fitting and testing the interaction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 12: Models with and without interaction m_sans <- lm(taille ~ sexe * nationalite, data = sans) m_avec <- lm(taille ~ sexe * nationalite, data = avec) anova(m_sans) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: taille Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) sexe 1 5441 5441 407.27 <2e-16 *** nationalite 1 3010 3010 225.31 <2e-16 *** sexe:nationalite 1 25 25 1.86 0.17 Residuals 156 2084 13 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_avec) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: taille Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) sexe 1 4829 4829 392.1 < 2e-16 *** nationalite 1 2807 2807 227.9 < 2e-16 *** sexe:nationalite 1 240 240 19.5 1.9e-05 *** Residuals 156 1921 12 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Compare nested models to assess the contribution of the interaction. anova(update(m_sans, . ~ . - sexe:nationalite), m_sans) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: taille ~ sexe + nationalite Model 2: taille ~ sexe * nationalite Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 157 2109 2 156 2084 1 24.8 1.86 0.17 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(update(m_avec, . ~ . - sexe:nationalite), m_avec) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: taille ~ sexe + nationalite Model 2: taille ~ sexe * nationalite Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 157 2161 2 156 1921 1 240 19.5 1.9e-05 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: Under the generating model without interaction, both expected differences are 12 cm. With interaction, they are 16 cm in A and 8 cm in B. The difference in differences is therefore $8-16=-8$ cm. # Experimental design: four fertilisers on 16 plots ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/proxy/320470/zhHpWm6LTfc9pU0c.mp4?width=1920&height=1080&start=0). ::: ## Experimental unit, replication and randomisation The experimental unit is the **plot** to which a fertiliser is assigned. Four plant measurements on the same plot do not become four independent treatment replicates. Randomisation limits allocation bias, while blocks control known heterogeneity. We consider two gradients: moisture increases along the rows, and sunlight along the columns. The yield values below are entirely simulated and expressed in an illustrative unit. ## Constructing the three designs ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 14: Experimental design set.seed(101) grille <- expand.grid(colonne = seq_len(4), ligne = seq_len(4)) # 1. Complete randomisation, with four replicates per fertiliser. aleatoire <- grille aleatoire$engrais <- sample(rep(LETTERS[1:4], each = 4)) # 2. Latin square: permute rows, columns and labels. carre_initial <- outer(0:3, 0:3, function(i, j) (i + j) %% 4 + 1) carre <- carre_initial[sample(4), sample(4)] etiquettes <- sample(LETTERS[1:4]) latin <- grille latin$engrais <- etiquettes[carre[cbind(latin$ligne, latin$colonne)]] # 3. Complete blocks: an independent permutation within each row. blocs <- grille blocs$engrais <- unlist(lapply(seq_len(4), function(i) sample(LETTERS[1:4]))) preparer <- function(z, nom) { z$plan <- nom z$humidite <- z$ligne z$ensoleillement <- z$colonne z$ligne <- factor(z$ligne) z$colonne <- factor(z$colonne) z$bloc <- z$ligne z$engrais <- factor(z$engrais, levels = LETTERS[1:4]) z } aleatoire <- preparer(aleatoire, "Completely randomised") latin <- preparer(latin, "Latin square") blocs <- preparer(blocs, "Complete blocks") stopifnot(all(table(aleatoire$engrais) == 4), all(table(latin$ligne, latin$engrais) == 1), all(table(latin$colonne, latin$engrais) == 1), all(table(blocs$bloc, blocs$engrais) == 1)) plans <- rbind(aleatoire, latin, blocs) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 15: Experimental design plot ggplot(plans, aes(colonne, ligne, fill = engrais)) + geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) + geom_text(aes(label = engrais), size = 6) + scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(levels(plans$ligne))) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel1") + coord_equal() + facet_wrap(~ plan) + labs(x = "Column: sunlight", y = "Row: moisture") + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Examples of randomised allocations. Moisture increases from top to bottom; sunlight increases from left to right.](index-en-r_files/figure-html/fig-plans-1.png){#fig-plans width=1056} ::: ::: | Design | Constraint | Classical model | Residual df without covariates | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | Completely randomised | 4 plots per fertiliser | `rendement ~ engrais` | 12 | | Latin square | Each fertiliser once per row and column | `rendement ~ engrais + ligne + colonne` | 6 | | Complete blocks | Each fertiliser once in each block | `rendement ~ engrais + bloc` | 9 | The Latin square controls two directions at the cost of degrees of freedom. There is only one observation per row–column combination: spatial interactions and interactions with treatments cannot be estimated separately in the classical model for this small design. The block design controls one direction without requiring balance across columns. ## Generating yields ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 16: Generated yields ajouter_rendement <- function(z, graine) { set.seed(graine) effet <- c(A = 0, B = 2, C = 4, D = 6) z$rendement <- 30 + unname(effet[as.character(z$engrais)]) + 2 * (z$humidite - 2.5) + 1.5 * (z$ensoleillement - 2.5) + rnorm(nrow(z), sd = 1.5) z } aleatoire <- ajouter_rendement(aleatoire, 201) latin <- ajouter_rendement(latin, 202) blocs <- ajouter_rendement(blocs, 203) knitr::kable(latin, digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |colonne |ligne |engrais |plan | humidite| ensoleillement|bloc | rendement| |:-------|:-----|:-------|:------------|--------:|--------------:|:----|---------:| |1 |1 |D |Latin square | 1| 1|1 | 29.05| |2 |1 |A |Latin square | 1| 2|1 | 25.59| |3 |1 |C |Latin square | 1| 3|1 | 31.25| |4 |1 |B |Latin square | 1| 4|1 | 29.98| |1 |2 |B |Latin square | 2| 1|2 | 28.53| |2 |2 |D |Latin square | 2| 2|2 | 32.10| |3 |2 |A |Latin square | 2| 3|2 | 28.59| |4 |2 |C |Latin square | 2| 4|2 | 32.35| |1 |3 |A |Latin square | 3| 1|3 | 29.22| |2 |3 |C |Latin square | 3| 2|3 | 34.95| |3 |3 |B |Latin square | 3| 3|3 | 33.54| |4 |3 |D |Latin square | 3| 4|3 | 41.02| |1 |4 |C |Latin square | 4| 1|4 | 33.59| |2 |4 |B |Latin square | 4| 2|4 | 34.09| |3 |4 |D |Latin square | 4| 3|4 | 42.25| |4 |4 |A |Latin square | 4| 4|4 | 34.86| ::: ::: These simulations share the same theoretical effects but have different errors. A single realisation is not enough to rank the designs by power. Comparing their performance would require repeating each experiment many times under specified scenarios. ## Analysing a completely randomised design ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 17: Randomised design m_aleatoire <- lm(rendement ~ engrais, data = aleatoire) anova(m_aleatoire) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: rendement Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) engrais 3 83.9 28.0 1.88 0.19 Residuals 12 178.4 14.9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Adjust for the measured gradients, assuming linear effects. m_ajuste <- lm(rendement ~ engrais + humidite + ensoleillement, data = aleatoire) anova(m_ajuste) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: rendement Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) engrais 3 83.9 28.0 16.1 0.00037 *** humidite 1 107.4 107.4 62.0 1.4e-05 *** ensoleillement 1 53.6 53.6 30.9 0.00024 *** Residuals 10 17.3 1.7 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} emmeans::emmeans(m_ajuste, pairwise ~ engrais, adjust = "tukey") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $emmeans engrais emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL A 29.5 0.676 10 28.0 31.0 B 30.8 0.662 10 29.3 32.3 C 34.6 0.658 10 33.1 36.0 D 36.3 0.681 10 34.8 37.8 Confidence level used: 0.95 $contrasts contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value A - B -1.31 0.946 10 -1.386 0.5349 A - C -5.11 0.944 10 -5.408 0.0014 A - D -6.83 0.985 10 -6.934 0.0002 B - C -3.79 0.934 10 -4.061 0.0103 B - D -5.52 0.956 10 -5.770 0.0009 C - D -1.72 0.947 10 -1.820 0.3194 P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates ``` ::: ::: Complete randomisation does not ensure exact balance of the gradients in an experiment with 16 plots. Covariates specified before the analysis can improve precision. The sequential order of the `anova` table must be taken into account; the adjusted fertiliser comparisons above use the full model. ## Analysing the Latin square ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 18: Latin square m_latin <- lm(rendement ~ engrais + ligne + colonne, data = latin) anova(m_latin) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: rendement Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) engrais 3 91.3 30.4 17.53 0.00226 ** ligne 3 141.4 47.1 27.14 0.00069 *** colonne 3 50.5 16.8 9.69 0.01024 * Residuals 6 10.4 1.7 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} emmeans::emmeans(m_latin, pairwise ~ engrais, adjust = "tukey") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $emmeans engrais emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL A 29.6 0.659 6 27.9 31.2 B 31.5 0.659 6 29.9 33.1 C 33.0 0.659 6 31.4 34.6 D 36.1 0.659 6 34.5 37.7 Results are averaged over the levels of: ligne, colonne Confidence level used: 0.95 $contrasts contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value A - B -1.97 0.932 6 -2.115 0.2490 A - C -3.47 0.932 6 -3.723 0.0371 A - D -6.54 0.932 6 -7.022 0.0017 B - C -1.50 0.932 6 -1.608 0.4406 B - D -4.57 0.932 6 -4.906 0.0107 C - D -3.07 0.932 6 -3.299 0.0604 Results are averaged over the levels of: ligne, colonne P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(df.residual(m_latin) == 6) ``` ::: Here, rows and columns are treated as fixed effects used to control variation. This is a classical analysis suited to the observed square. Treating them as random effects involves a different assumption about the population they come from, discussed below. ## Analysing complete blocks ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 19: Block design m_blocs <- lm(rendement ~ engrais + bloc, data = blocs) anova(m_blocs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Response: rendement Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) engrais 3 183.3 61.1 19.87 0.00026 *** bloc 3 80.9 27.0 8.77 0.00490 ** Residuals 9 27.7 3.1 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} emmeans::emmeans(m_blocs, pairwise ~ engrais, adjust = "tukey") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $emmeans engrais emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL A 30.2 0.877 9 28.2 32.2 B 28.6 0.877 9 26.7 30.6 C 36.2 0.877 9 34.2 38.2 D 36.0 0.877 9 34.0 38.0 Results are averaged over the levels of: bloc Confidence level used: 0.95 $contrasts contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value A - B 1.580 1.24 9 1.275 0.5995 A - C -5.980 1.24 9 -4.823 0.0043 A - D -5.789 1.24 9 -4.669 0.0053 B - C -7.560 1.24 9 -6.098 0.0008 B - D -7.369 1.24 9 -5.944 0.0010 C - D 0.191 1.24 9 0.154 0.9986 Results are averaged over the levels of: bloc P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates ``` ::: ::: Treatments are compared while accounting for differences between blocks. If the blocks are the only levels of interest, a fixed effect is a natural choice. If they represent exchangeable units from a population of blocks, a random effect may be suitable. # Linear mixed models (LMM) ## Fixed and random effects A fixed effect describes differences between specific levels we want to compare, such as the four fertilisers. A random intercept describes variation between grouped units, such as sites or blocks considered exchangeable. Observations in the same group share this intercept and are therefore marginally correlated. For the block design: $$Y_{bk}=\mu+\alpha_k+u_b+\varepsilon_{bk},\qquad u_b\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_b^2),\quad \varepsilon_{bk}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).$$ Random effects are assumed to be independent of the errors and predictors. The exchangeability assumption needs careful consideration: rows ordered along a gradient may be better described by a measured covariate than by independent intercepts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 20: Mixed model m_mixte <- lmerTest::lmer(rendement ~ engrais + (1 | bloc), data = blocs) summary(m_mixte) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [ lmerModLmerTest] Formula: rendement ~ engrais + (1 | bloc) Data: blocs REML criterion at convergence: 59.6 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.712 -0.418 0.162 0.510 1.233 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. bloc (Intercept) 5.97 2.44 Residual 3.07 1.75 Number of obs: 16, groups: bloc, 4 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error df t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 30.22 1.50 5.20 20.10 3.9e-06 *** engraisB -1.58 1.24 9.00 -1.27 0.23433 engraisC 5.98 1.24 9.00 4.82 0.00094 *** engraisD 5.79 1.24 9.00 4.67 0.00117 ** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Correlation of Fixed Effects: (Intr) engrsB engrsC engraisB -0.412 engraisC -0.412 0.500 engraisD -0.412 0.500 0.500 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Approximate F-tests, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. anova(m_mixte, ddf = "Satterthwaite") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Type III Analysis of Variance Table with Satterthwaite's method Sum Sq Mean Sq NumDF DenDF F value Pr(>F) engrais 183 61.1 3 9 19.9 0.00026 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(m_mixte)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` grp var1 var2 vcov sdcor 1 bloc (Intercept) 5.972 2.444 2 Residual 3.074 1.753 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lme4::isSingular(m_mixte) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} emmeans::emmeans(m_mixte, pairwise ~ engrais, adjust = "tukey", lmer.df = "satterthwaite") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $emmeans engrais emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL A 30.2 1.5 5.2 26.4 34.0 B 28.6 1.5 5.2 24.8 32.5 C 36.2 1.5 5.2 32.4 40.0 D 36.0 1.5 5.2 32.2 39.8 Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite Confidence level used: 0.95 $contrasts contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value A - B 1.580 1.24 9 1.275 0.5995 A - C -5.980 1.24 9 -4.823 0.0043 A - D -5.789 1.24 9 -4.669 0.0053 B - C -7.560 1.24 9 -6.098 0.0008 B - D -7.369 1.24 9 -5.944 0.0010 C - D 0.191 1.24 9 0.154 0.9986 Degrees-of-freedom method: satterthwaite P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates ``` ::: ::: With only four blocks, the between-block variance is difficult to estimate reliably. A singular fit can indicate a variance estimated at the boundary, often close to zero. This calls for reassessing the model and design; it is not proof that there is no biological variability. ## Crossed effects in the Latin square ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 21: Latin square m_latin_mixte <- lmerTest::lmer( rendement ~ engrais + (1 | ligne) + (1 | colonne), data = latin) summary(m_latin_mixte) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [ lmerModLmerTest] Formula: rendement ~ engrais + (1 | ligne) + (1 | colonne) Data: latin REML criterion at convergence: 62.9 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.0512 -0.3587 -0.0346 0.3901 1.0891 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ligne (Intercept) 11.35 3.37 colonne (Intercept) 3.77 1.94 Residual 1.74 1.32 Number of obs: 16, groups: ligne, 4; colonne, 4 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error df t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 29.564 2.053 5.433 14.40 1.6e-05 *** engraisB 1.971 0.932 6.000 2.12 0.07878 . engraisC 3.469 0.932 6.000 3.72 0.00982 ** engraisD 6.544 0.932 6.000 7.02 0.00042 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Correlation of Fixed Effects: (Intr) engrsB engrsC engraisB -0.227 engraisC -0.227 0.500 engraisD -0.227 0.500 0.500 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lme4::isSingular(m_latin_mixte) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: The row and column effects are **crossed**, because every row meets every column. This is the model shown in the PPTX, but its use depends on how the rows and columns are regarded. It remains additive and does not overcome the lack of replication needed to identify all interactions. With four levels per random effect, report the uncertainty and consider the fixed-effects analysis. ## Diagnostics and within-group correlation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 22: Diagnostics ancien <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(fitted(m_mixte), residuals(m_mixte), xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Conditional residual") abline(h = 0, lty = 2) qqnorm(residuals(m_mixte)); qqline(residuals(m_mixte)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/diagnostic-mixte-1.png){width=864} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(ancien) vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(m_mixte)) variance_bloc <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "bloc"] variance_erreur <- sigma(m_mixte)^2 icc <- variance_bloc / (variance_bloc + variance_erreur) icc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6602 ``` ::: ::: The ICC is the proportion of variance attributed to the block in this random-intercept model. Its estimate is highly uncertain here. To compare models with different fixed effects using a likelihood-ratio test, refit them with `REML = FALSE`; do not compare their REML likelihoods directly. # Bootstrap: estimating uncertainty by resampling ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}

``` [Open the video](https://mediaserver.unige.ch/proxy/320473/k6IAaXNp5HPrrVJH.mp4?width=1920&height=1080&start=0). ::: ## The principle Starting from $n$ observations, we draw $n$ observations **with replacement**. Some appear several times, while others are absent. We recalculate a statistic and repeat this process $B$ times. The resulting distribution approximates the statistic’s sampling distribution under the assumptions of the resampling procedure. Bootstrap does not create new independent individuals or correct a biased sample. It does not require normally distributed observations in these examples, but it depends, among other things, on representativeness and the dependence structure. A small sample may represent extreme values poorly. ## Visualising one draw with replacement ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 23: Bootstrap set.seed(7) x <- c(158, 162, 165, 168, 170, 172, 174, 177, 179, 184) indices <- sample.int(length(x), size = length(x), replace = TRUE) knitr::kable(data.frame(draw_position = seq_along(x), sampled_individual = indices, sampled_height = x[indices])) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | draw_position| sampled_individual| sampled_height| |-------------:|------------------:|--------------:| | 1| 10| 184| | 2| 3| 165| | 3| 7| 174| | 4| 2| 162| | 5| 10| 184| | 6| 6| 172| | 7| 8| 177| | 8| 8| 177| | 9| 3| 165| | 10| 8| 177| ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(original_mean = mean(x), resample_mean = mean(x[indices])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` original_mean resample_mean 170.9 173.7 ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution of the mean and percentile confidence interval ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 24: Bootstrap for height set.seed(7) B <- 2000 b <- replicate(B, mean(sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE))) ic <- quantile(b, c(.025, .975)) knitr::kable(data.frame(estimate = mean(x), bootstrap_mean = mean(b), estimated_bias = mean(b) - mean(x), bootstrap_standard_error = sd(b), lower_025 = ic[1], upper_975 = ic[2]), row.names = FALSE, digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | estimate| bootstrap_mean| estimated_bias| bootstrap_standard_error| lower_025| upper_975| |--------:|--------------:|--------------:|------------------------:|---------:|---------:| | 170.9| 170.9| -0.02| 2.41| 166.2| 175.7| ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data.frame(moyenne = b), aes(moyenne)) + geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "#367CA5", color = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(x), linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = ic, linetype = 2, color = "#BB4B32") + labs(x = "Bootstrap mean height (cm)", y = "Number of resamples") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index-en-r_files/figure-html/bootstrap-tailles-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The dashed lines mark the 95% percentile confidence interval. If the entire sampling and calculation procedure were ideally repeated, a well-calibrated method would cover the parameter in about 95% of cases. This does not assign a 95% probability to the fixed parameter after observing this particular interval. ## Returning to the workbook data We use the mean of `lex` among the available African countries. This is still a mean **across countries**. The interval illustrates what a model of independent, exchangeable countries would produce; it does not correct for geographical dependence. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 25: Bootstrap for countries xaf <- d$lex[d$region == "africa"] stopifnot(length(xaf) > 2) set.seed(301) B <- 4999 baf <- replicate(B, mean(sample(xaf, length(xaf), replace = TRUE))) knitr::kable(data.frame(n = length(xaf), mean = mean(xaf), bootstrap_se = sd(baf), lower = unname(quantile(baf, .025)), upper = unname(quantile(baf, .975))), digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | n| mean| bootstrap_se| lower| upper| |--:|-----:|------------:|-----:|-----:| | 54| 66.43| 0.72| 65.06| 67.84| ::: ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(xaf)$conf.int ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 64.99 67.87 attr(,"conf.level") [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ::: Compare the bootstrap interval with the one based on the t distribution. Similarity does not establish that all assumptions are satisfied. Increasing $B$ makes the numerical quantile estimates more stable without increasing the number of countries or removing bias in the data. ## BCa confidence intervals with the boot package The PPTX also presents a BCa interval. Bias and acceleration corrections account for some forms of asymmetry; the BCa interval may differ from the percentile interval. Neither guarantees correct coverage for every distribution or every small sample. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Block 26: Bootstrap quantile intervals set.seed(302) stat_moyenne <- function(donnees, indices) mean(donnees[indices]) objet_boot <- boot::boot(data = xaf, statistic = stat_moyenne, R = 4999) objet_boot ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ORDINARY NONPARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP Call: boot::boot(data = xaf, statistic = stat_moyenne, R = 4999) Bootstrap Statistics : original bias std. error t1* 66.43 0.01005 0.6966 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} boot::boot.ci(objet_boot, type = c("perc", "bca")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` BOOTSTRAP CONFIDENCE INTERVAL CALCULATIONS Based on 4999 bootstrap replicates CALL : boot::boot.ci(boot.out = objet_boot, type = c("perc", "bca")) Intervals : Level Percentile BCa 95% (65.06, 67.84 ) (65.10, 67.88 ) Calculations and Intervals on Original Scale ``` ::: ::: # Summary: choosing a coherent approach ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{=html}
